record.paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
record.original_question: What is the computational complexity of the decision conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups, for example for the Eick-Ostheimer algorithm?

evidence.quote: 2. What is the complexity of the decision conjugacy problem, for example in Eick-Ostheimer algorithm [EO]?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called polycyclic if it admits a subnormal series
$$G = G_0 \trianglerighteq G_1 \trianglerighteq \cdots \trianglerighteq G_n = \{1\}$$
in which every quotient $G_i/G_{i+1}$ is cyclic. Every polycyclic group is finitely presented and admits a polycyclic presentation, with respect to which group elements have a unique normal form. The decision conjugacy problem in $G$ asks: given two elements $u, v \in G$ (encoded by their normal forms), decide whether there exists $g \in G$ such that $g^{-1} u g = v$.

It is known that the decision conjugacy problem is solvable for every polycyclic group, and concrete algorithms (such as the one of Eick and Ostheimer, which reduces the problem to computations involving unit groups and orbit-stabilizer problems in algebraic number fields and matrix groups) realize such a decision procedure.

Determine the computational complexity of the decision conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups. In particular, give a rigorous worst-case complexity analysis (as a function of the input size, e.g.\ the bit-length of the polycyclic presentation together with the input elements) of the Eick–Ostheimer conjugacy algorithm.
artifact.status_search_result: A complete worst-case complexity analysis of the Eick–Ostheimer algorithm itself does not appear to have been carried out; experimental studies (Eick–Kahrobaei) showed the running time grows rapidly with Hirsch length. On the structural side, partial progress is available: Cavallo and Kahrobaei (2014, arXiv:1403.4153) exhibit a family of polycyclic groups for which the (uniform) conjugacy problem is NP-complete, showing that no polynomial-time algorithm is possible in general unless P = NP. The general status of the precise complexity of the decision conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups remains an open problem in the polycyclic-group cryptography literature.
